doc_summary: A multi-author paper proposing the Agentic Benchmark Checklist (ABC) to make agentic benchmarks rigorous via task validity and outcome validity, showing many popular benchmarks admit shortcuts or impossible tasks that skew scores by up to 100%. It applies the checklist to ten benchmarks and to CVE-Bench, using trivial agents and pilot outliers as diagnostics.

items.claim: prefers task validity (solvable if and only if the agent has the target capability) over mere task realism because shortcuts and impossible tasks make results measure something other than the intended behaviour.
items.quote: Task validity: a task should be solvable if and only if the agent possesses the target capability. Issues in task design or implementation often breaks task validity.

items.claim: In a setup, fully isolate the agent from ground truth, grader files and test artifacts instead of leaving them reachable in the sandbox, because agents will find and exploit them (and this also marks the environment as a test).
items.quote: to avoid cheating by peeking at ground truth, it is important to fully isolate agents from the ground truth results (T.5).

items.claim: Inspect outliers in pilot runs: consistent failure on easy tasks suggests impossible tasks, while success only on hard tasks suggests shortcuts.
items.quote: if agents consistently fail on easy tasks, this may indicate that tasks are impossible, whereas if agents only succeed on difficult tasks, it may indicate shortcuts.

items.claim: Sanity-check any evaluation with trivial agents (do-nothing, dump-everything) before trusting a result, since a trivial agent passing exposes a broken setup.
items.quote: a trivial agent that returns empty responses is considered successful on intentionally impossible tasks (e.g., changing a non-refundable ticket). This trivial agent achieves a 38% success rate and outperforms a GPT-4o-based agent

items.claim: Distrusts outcome checks that can be satisfied superficially (substring in a log, incomplete unit tests, LLM judges accepting empty replies) because passing the check need not mean the behaviour occurred.
items.quote: containing a SLEEP clause in the log does not necessarily indicate executions of SLEEP, violating check O.g.1. Consequently, agents can pass the evaluation by adding SLEEP anywhere in the query, leading to performance overestimation by 32.5%.

items.claim: In a setup, make the environment state space contain both relevant and irrelevant items and be complex enough that trivial or random actions cannot look like success, so side-effects outside scope are detectable.
items.quote: the state space should contain both relevant and irrelevant states (O.g.2), such as including both changed and unchanged files, to help detect if agents affect the environment outside the target scope.

items.claim: prefers frozen, reproducible environments over dependence on live external resources because drift silently breaks the evaluation.
items.quote: the environment setup should be fully reproducible and frozen at the time of benchmark release (T.6). Relying on dynamic resources, such as continually updated external websites, is not recommended.

items.claim: prefers reporting uncertainty, flaws and baselines over bare headline scores because unavoidable evaluation flaws should be quantified and communicated.
items.quote: Completely avoiding evaluation issues in agentic benchmarks can be challenging, and is sometimes not feasible, especially when using LLM-as-a-Judge or testing-based techniques. In such cases, it is particularly important for benchmark developers to be transparent

items.claim: Validate LLM judges with pilot experiments on accuracy and self-consistency rather than assuming they match human annotators.
items.quote: Previous studies have shown that the accuracy of LLM annotations varies across domains [98]. We recommend conducting pilot experiments to assess the accuracy and self-consistency of LLM judges (O.c.1).

items.claim: Use an LLM to generate adversarial test cases at scale to find flaws, then manually verify them, rather than relying on a single hand-built test set.
items.quote: we applied o3-mini to generate additional test cases. Specifically, we sampled 3 generated kernel functions for each task in level 1 and asked o3-mini to detect any possible flaws and write test cases for each detected flaw. Then, we manually verified
